title: The History of Palm Oil — The World's Most Invisible Ingredient
fullText: You used it this morning. You probably touched it at least three times before you left the house. It was in your toothpaste. It was in your shampoo. If you ate something out of a package for breakfast, it was almost certainly in that, too. [music] And yet, if someone asked you to find it on the ingredient label, you would have a very hard time because this particular ingredient goes by more than 200 names. Sodium laurel sulfate, glycerol sterate, steeric acid, settle alcohol, palmitate, alas gininesis. All of those names [music] and dozens more point back to the same crop. Palm oil. It is the most widely consumed vegetable oil on the planet [music] accounting for roughly a third of all vegetable oil production worldwide. A 2025 study led by Emily Majard of Borneo Futures checked the ingredient labels of 1,600 products across three major supermarket chains in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Australia. Only about 8% of packaged products actually listed palm oil by name. But when the researchers accounted for unspecified vegetable oils and chemical derivatives that are commonly sourced from palm, the real number climbed to as high as 40%. What nobody knew for most of human history was that this quiet ingredient from the forests of West Africa would become one of the most fought over commodities on Earth. But this story does not start on a supermarket shelf. It starts in the tropical rainforests along [music] the Gulf of Guinea thousands of years before anyone called it a commodity. The oil palm tree Ela Ginensis is indigenous to West Africa. It grows naturally in a [music] belt that runs through what is now Nigeria, Cameroon, Ghana, Sierra Leon, Liberia, [music] Togo, and down into the Congo basin. And the relationship between this tree and the people who lived around it is ancient. Archaeological evidence shows that West Africans were using palm fruit and palm kernel oil as part of their diet at least [music] 5,000 years ago. The oil was deep red, rich in flavor, and packed with nutrients. And it served almost every function a household needed. Women cooked with it. Families used it for soap. Communities burned it in lamps for light. It was rubbed into skin and hair as a moisturizer. In some West African traditions, palm oil carried spiritual significance, too. Used in ceremonies and rituals [music] as a symbol of vitality and abundance. The trees themselves were remarkably cooperative. Oil palms thrived in cleared and burned areas, which meant that [music] wherever humans farmed and moved on, palm groves would spring up in the abandoned land. Old village sites [music] and former farm camps became dense clusters of palm trees over the years. So much so that even today, the distribution of wild oil palms across West Africa [music] maps almost perfectly onto the locations of ancient settlements. You can walk through a stretch of forest in what is now southern Nigeria or [music] Cameroon and read the history of human habitation just by looking at where the palms grow. That relationship [music] between people and tree shaped both. Human migration spread the palm. The palm in turn fed the communities that followed. Processing [music] the fruit into oil was labor inensive work carried out almost [music] entirely by women. They would collect the ripe fruit, boil it repeatedly, pound it, then filter the mixture by hand with water, skimming the red oil from the surface as it separated. It was slow, physically demanding, [music] and remarkably effective. The method had not changed much in thousands of years and variations of it are still used across West Africa today. While the red oil came from the fleshy outer layer of the fruit, women also cracked open the hard palm kernels, sometimes with the help of [music] children, to extract a different oil, a lighter, clearer brown kernel oil used for [music] different purposes. From the simplest village dish of boiled yam with palm oil and salt to the elaborate stews and soups of the Niger Delta and the Yoruba regions, this oil was woven into the fabric of daily life. The Euroba even developed a famous black [music] soap called dudu oen made with palm oil and wood ash, a product that is still manufactured [music] and sold as a Nigerian brand today. European traders first encountered palm oil when they arrived on the Guinea coast in the 15th century. They noticed how central it was to local [music] diets and local economies. But for the next 300 years, they mostly ignored it as a serious trade good. The reason was grim. There was far more money in the slave trade. Palm oil was bulky and cheap compared to the profits available from trafficking human beings across the Atlantic. Merchants did buy small quantities, sometimes using it as food for enslaved people during the Middle Passage. But in the ledgers of European commerce, palm oil barely registered as a footnote. Meanwhile, in the late 19th century, chemists in Europe made a discovery that would quietly reshape the entire [music] vegetable oil industry. They found that hydrogenation, a process of adding [music] hydrogen to liquid unsaturated fats, could turn vegetable oils into solid fats. That meant you [music] could take a liquid oil like palm and convert it into something that behaved [music] like butter. The result was margarine and margarine was about to become one of the most important foods in industrializing Europe. The growing urban working class needed cheap calorie dense fats and margarine could be mass-roduced at a fraction of the cost of butter. This discovery did not immediately change the [music] palm oil trade but it set the stage for everything that came later. It meant palm [music] oil was no longer just useful for soap and lubrication. It was also useful for food at an industrial scale. That changed in 1807 when Britain abolished the Atlantic slave trade. The network of British traders operating along the West African coast suddenly needed a new commodity. Palm oil was the obvious answer. The infrastructure was already [music] there. The traders already knew the local brokers and river roots. And back in Europe, demand for fats and oils was surging. The industrial revolution had created enormous new needs that animal fats alone could not meet. Factories required lubricants for their machinery. The tin plate industry needed processing [music] oil and palm oil turned out to be perfectly suited for it. The growing urban populations of London, Manchester, and [music] Liverpool wanted affordable soap and candles, products that had traditionally been made from animal fats like tallow [music] and lard, supplies that were increasingly difficult to secure. At the scale that industrial cities demanded, palm oil stepped into that gap. The British government [music] actively encouraged the transition. In 1845, it abolished the import duty on palm oil entirely, making it even cheaper to bring into the country and signaling to traders that this was the commodity of the future. By the 1870s, palm oil had become the primary export of several West African nations. In the Niger Delta alone, exports reached 25,000 to 30,000 tons per year. The trade reshaped political power across the region. Powerful African brokers built entire states around it. King Jaja of Oppobo is one of the most striking examples. Born into slavery among the [music] Igbo people, Jaja rose through the ranks of the palm oil trade, eventually founding his own independent state [music] called Oppobbo, which became one of the largest European trading stations on the West African coast. [music] At his peak, Ja commanded fleets of 300 to 400 large trading canoes. Each one capable of carrying up to 2400 gallons [music] of palm oil. That is a staggering volume of trade for a single broker. And it gives you a sense of just how valuable this oil had become. Then in 1885, two brothers in the English town of Warrington made a decision that would change the palm oil story forever. William Heskath Lever and his brother James Darcy Lever bought a small soap works and partnered with a chemist [music] named William Huff Watson. Watson had developed a new soap making process that [music] used glycerin and vegetable oils, particularly palm oil, instead of the animal tallow [music] that most soap makers relied on. The result was a product that lthered more easily, smelled better, and could be manufactured cheaply at enormous scale. They originally called it honey soap then renamed it sunlight soap and William Lever turned out to be one of the great marketers [music] of the 19th century. Within a decade, Sunlight Soap was on sale in 134 countries. By 1888, the factory was producing 450 tons of soap every single week. Business was growing so fast that Lever bought a large piece of marshland on the Whirl Peninsula near Liverpool and built an entire purpose-built village for his workers, complete with housing, schools, recreational facilities, and a church. He called it Port Sunlight. It was a model industrial community, and every brick of it was paid for by palm oil. Lever did not [music] stop at Sunlight Soap. As public interest in hygiene grew, the company launched LifeBoy, a soap that used carbolic acid [music] to fight germs, but was priced low enough for workingclass families to afford. Then came Lux, then Vim. Each product was marketed aggressively, and each one ran on the same raw material. By the turn of the century, Lever Brothers was one of the largest consumer goods companies in Britain, and Palm oil was the engine behind all of it. But Lever had a problem that would not go away. As demand for his soap grew, he needed a reliable, enormous supply of raw palm oil, and he did not want to depend on West African brokers who could set their own prices and negotiate hard. So he went directly to the source. In the early 1900s, William Lever bought oil palm plantations in the Solomon Islands. Then in 1911 he secured a concession from the Belgian colonial government in the Congo establishing a subsidiary called Wheeleries Dongo Belge. The name sounds like a bureaucratic entry in a business register. The reality was brutal. The plantations in the Congo operated using forced labor. local people compelled to harvest palm fruit under coercive conditions, feeding a supply chain that terminated in the bathrooms and kitchens of middle-class British households. If you used sunlight soap [music] or life boy or lux in the early 20th century, the oil in that bar very likely passed through the hands of forced laborers in central Africa. That connection was not advertised. [music] World War I accelerated the company's growth even further. A British naval blockade cut German mills off from their vegetable oil sources in West Africa and many of those supplies were diverted to lever brothers instead. The company moved into margarine production because soap and margarine share the same fundamental raw ingredient, vegetable oil, and there was another link to the war effort. A byproduct of soap making is glycerin, which is a key ingredient in explosives. [music] Lever brothers delivered glycerin to British arms manufacturers throughout the war. In 1917, in recognition of his contributions, William Lever was made a life pier and became [music] Lord Lever. His soap empire built on palm oil had helped arm a nation. By the late 1920s, Lever Brothers was not the only company hungry for vegetable oils. Across the English Channel, the Dutch margarine industry had produced its own giants. Back in 1871, the Jurgens family had acquired [music] the original patent for making margarine from its French inventor, and they had built a massive business around it. Meanwhile, the Vanberg family was running a competing margarine empire with a sales force of 750 people and growing export operations across [music] Europe. Both families were buying palm oil and other vegetable oils from West Africa, Nigeria, and Salon, and they had been competing fiercely for the same raw materials for years. Since soap companies [music] and margarine companies were both fighting over the exact same vegetable oils, a merger started to make strategic sense. In 1929, Lever Brothers merged with the Dutch conglomerate [music] Margarine Uni to form Unilver. It was one of the largest corporate mergers in European history. At its founding, Unilver employed 250,000 people. The company that would eventually own Dove, Helman's, Ben and Jerry's, Canor, and hundreds of other brands was born at its root from the economics [music] of palm oil. Soap on one side, margarine on the other, and palm oil connecting them both. For most of the 20th century, West Africa remained the center of palm oil production. But the center of gravity was about to shift halfway around the world and the shift would be [music] dramatic. In the 1960s, global rubber prices collapsed [music] and Malaysia, which had built much of its economy around rubber plantations, needed a replacement crop urgently. Oil palm fit the bill. Malaysia had the tropical climate. It had vast amounts of arable [music] land, much of it already cleared for rubber, and it had the institutional capacity to build a modern plantation industry quickly. The government launched programs to convert old rubber estates to oil palm, resettling farmers onto organized plantation schemes and establishing research institutions to develop higher yielding palm varieties. Much of this early expansion happened on land that had already been cleared for rubber, which reduced the immediate environmental cost. Production climbed steadily through the 70s and 80s. By the mid 1980s, Malaysia had overtaken every West African producer [music] to become the largest palm oil exporter on Earth. The country that had inherited its first oil palm seeds from West Africa [music] only decades earlier was now shipping millions of tons of palm oil to India, China, Europe, and beyond. And it was about to get [music] company. Indonesia watched Malaysia's success closely and then followed but on a vastly larger scale through government policies that actively encouraged agricultural expansion particularly on the islands of Sumatra, [music] Kalimantan, and Sulawesi. Indonesia began converting enormous tracks of land to oil palm plantations starting in the early 1990s. The numbers are difficult to wrap your head around. Indonesia's total oil palm plantation area grew from 5.3 million hectares [music] in 2003 to over 16 million hectares by [music] the end of 2024. That is a more than three-fold expansion in just two [music] decades. By 2024, Indonesia was producing roughly 43 million tons of crude palm oil per year. Malaysia added another [music] 19.7 million tons. Together, the two countries accounted for [music] 82.2% of all palm oil produced on Earth. Global production in 2024 reached 76.3 [music] million tons total. Palm oil had gone from a regional cooking ingredient to the backbone of global food manufacturing in less than a century. India alone imported over 20% of the [music] world's supply. China took another 10%. The European Union, for all its environmental concerns, [music] imported close to 9%. And the United States, where palm oil imports have surged by hundreds of percent over the past two decades, was consuming more than ever before. So why palm oil specifically? Why not soy or sunflower or rape seed or coconut? The answer comes down to yield and versatility, and both are hard to argue with. An oil palm plantation produces 5 to 10 times more oil per hectare than any other major oil crop. To get the same amount of oil from soybeans, you would need roughly [music] 6 to 10 times as much farmland. Palm oil is also uniquely functional. It is semi-olid at [music] room temperature, which makes it perfect for spreads and baked goods that need to hold their shape [music] without refrigeration. It is resistant to oxidation, which gives products a longer shelf life. [music] It is stable at very high temperatures, which is why fried foods made with palm oil come out crispy and hold their texture. And it is both odless and colorless, which means it disappears into whatever product it enters without changing the taste, the look, or the smell. That combination of extreme efficiency and extreme versatility is what made palm oil essentially irreplaceable in the modern food system. It is not just that it is cheap. It is that nothing else does all the same things while using so little land. But the cost of that expansion has been enormous. Between 1997 and 2006, [music] palm oil deforestation in Indonesia reached a peak of roughly 400,000 [music] hectares per year. That is about a million acres of forest cleared annually. Much of it tropical rainforest and carbonrich petland on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. These are not ordinary [music] forests. They are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on the planet. [music] Home to species found nowhere else on Earth. Sumatran tigers, Sumatran rhinoceroses, sunbears, pygmy elephants, [music] clouded leopards, and orangutans. The orangutan has become the face [music] of the palm oil crisis, and the numbers make it clear why. In the early 1900s, more than 300,000 [music] orangutans lived in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. Then the clearing began. A comprehensive [music] study published in the journal Current Biology conducted by researchers from the Maxplank Institute [music] for Evolutionary Anthropology and other institutions estimated that the Bornean Orangutang population dropped by more than 100,000 individuals between 1999 and [music] 2015. The most dramatic declines occurred in areas where tropical forest was cut [music] down and converted directly into oil palm plantations. Orangutans are slow breeders. A female gives birth on average once every 8 years and raises no more than three offspring in her entire lifetime. When you destroy habitat at industrial speed and the species living in it reproduces at generational speed, the math does not work in the animals favor. The Borneian orangutan is now classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. The Sumatran orangutan with a population [music] of roughly 14,000 is in even more precarious territory. And in 2017, scientists identified a third species, the Tapani orangutang, also in Sumatra with fewer than 800 individuals remaining. The deforestation does not only affect wildlife. When tropical petlands are drained and cleared for plantations, the carbon stored in those soils. Carbon that accumulated over thousands of years gets released into the atmosphere. Pete soils in Southeast Asia can be meters deep and they hold vastly more carbon per hectare than regular tropical forest soil. Drain the [music] pete, expose it to air, and it begins to decompose and release carbon dioxide. set it on fire [music] and the release is catastrophic. Indonesia's fire seasons, particularly in 1997 and again in 2015, were exactly that. [music] In 2015, fires burned across Sumatra and Kalimantan for months, blanketing cities in a toxic haze that shut [music] down schools, grounded flights, and sent tens of thousands of people to hospitals with respiratory problems. The smoke spread across international borders into Singapore and Malaysia, triggering diplomatic tensions [music] between the countries. Singapore's air quality index spiked into hazardous territory for days at a time, [music] and the Malaysian government declared states of emergency in several regions. Satellite data showed that on some days during that crisis, Indonesia's daily greenhouse [music] gas emissions from the fires exceeded those of the entire United States economy. The fires were not accidents [music] of nature. They were the result of slash and burn clearing for plantations, a practice [music] that was faster and cheaper than mechanical land clearing and one that had been banned repeatedly on paper but continued on the ground. So the environmental case against palm oil seems straightforward. Stop buying it. Boycott it. Choose products labeled palm oil free. But the picture is far more complicated [music] than that. And this is where the story resists a clean ending. First, there is the land use math and it is unforgiving. [music] If the world replaced all its palm oil with soybean oil, rape seed oil, or [music] sunflower oil tomorrow, it would need vastly more farmland to produce the same volume of oil because those crops yield so much less per hectare. Some estimates suggest you would [music] need 4 to 10 times as much land depending on the replacement crop. That additional farmland would [music] have to come from somewhere. In the case of soy, the most likely candidate, it would almost certainly mean expanding [music] soybean cultivation into the Amazon basin, the Sarado grasslands of Brazil, or [music] the Grand Choco in Argentina, ecosystems that are already under intense pressure from agricultural expansion. The deforestation problem would not disappear. It would move to [music] different continents and affect different ecosystems, potentially even larger ones. This is the trap [music] that makes palm oil so hard to quit. The crop is efficient enough that replacing it could actually cause more environmental damage, not less. Second, there are the people. Palm oil is not just a corporate commodity traded on commodity exchanges by multinational conglomerates. In Indonesia alone, millions of smallh holder farmers depend on oil palm for their income. The sector contributes roughly 4 and a half% of Indonesia's entire gross domestic product and supports the livelihoods of rural communities across Sumatra and Calamantan. For many of these families, switching to a different crop is not a realistic option. Their land is planted, their trees are mature, their buyers are established. Telling them to stop growing palm oil is easy from a supermarket aisle in London or a grocery store in New York. It looks very [music] different from a small holding in Rial Province where the nearest alternative income might [music] be hours away. Third, there is the labeling problem. The thing that brought us into this story in the first place. Even consumers who genuinely want to make informed choices face an almost impossible task. Palm oil derivatives show up on ingredient lists under names that give absolutely no hint of their origin. Settle alcohol, sodium laurith sulfate, steeric acid, glycerol sterate, palm oil tetropeptide. The list goes on and on. In most [music] countries, manufacturers are not required to specify whether a vegetable oil or oliochemical ingredient comes from palm, soy, coconut, or something else entirely. You can scrutinize every label in the store, [music] spend 20 minutes in the shampoo aisle reading the fine print, and still walk out with no idea what you are actually buying or where it came from. The most significant industry response to all of this has been the push for sustainable production rather than outright elimination. The movement gained momentum in the aftermath of the 1997 fires, which were so devastating that they forced governments, corporations, and environmental organizations [music] to acknowledge that business as usual was not sustainable. Years of negotiations followed. Then in 2004, the roundt on sustainable palm oil was formally established in Zurich, [music] Switzerland. Its founding members included the World Wildlife Fund, Unilver, the Malaysian Palm Oil Association, the Swedish Danish Company, AAK, [music] and the Swiss retailer Migros. The idea was to create a voluntary certification system that would set environmental and [music] social standards for palm oil production, covering everything from deforestation protections to labor rights to community relations. Producers who met the standards could sell certified sustainable palm oil and charge a premium for it. Today, the RSPO has grown to more than 6,000 members [music] across 94 countries. About 20% of global palm oil production is now certified under its standards. [music] Critics say 20% is not nearly enough, that the certification process [music] has real enforcement gaps, and that the RSPO has sometimes allowed members to continue clearing land while remaining [music] certified. Supporters counter that voluntary certification, imperfect as it is, remains the only realistic path forward for an industry this large, [music] and that holding palm oil to standards that no other vegetable oil is held to is inconsistent at best and [music] counterproductive at worst. The European Union has taken a more regulatory approach, passing a deforestation regulation that requires importers [music] to prove their commodities, including palm oil, are not linked to [music] recent forest clearing. Indonesia and Malaysia have pushed back hard, arguing that the regulation [music] unfairly penalizes developing nations whose forests are still standing while overlooking the fact that Europe cleared its own forests centuries ago to build the agricultural wealth it now enjoys. That argument, [music] like the others, has a point. What started 5,000 years ago as a red oil skimmed from boiled fruit by women along the rivers of West Africa has become a substance woven into the invisible infrastructure of modern life. It is in bread and ice cream and instant [music] noodles. It is in lipstick and laundry detergent and biodiesel fuel. It is produced on a scale that would have been unimaginable to the communities who first cultivated it. Traded by [music] corporations whose origins trace directly back to the colonial extraction of African resources, it has created fortunes and destroyed forests. It feeds billions of people and threatens species with extinction. It employs millions of farmers and displaces indigenous communities. It is the most efficient oil crop ever cultivated [music] and the most controversial. and it sits on your shelf right now, invisible under a name you would never recognize. The real question is not whether palm oil is good or bad. It is whether the systems that produce it, the supply chains that disguise it, and the markets that demand it can be [music] reformed fast enough to matter before the forests and the species that depend [music] on them run out of time. Dầu có màu đỏ đậm, giàu hương vị và chứa nhiều chất dinh dưỡng. Và nó phục vụ hầu hết mọi chức năng mà một hộ gia đình cần. Phụ nữ nấu ăn với nó. Các gia đình sử dụng nó để làm xà phòng. Cộng đồng đốt nó trong đèn để lấy ánh sáng. Nó được xoa vào da và tóc như một loại kem dưỡng ẩm. Trong một số truyền thống Tây Phi, dầu cọ cũng mang ý nghĩa tâm linh. Được sử dụng trong các nghi lễ, nghi lễ [âm nhạc] như biểu tượng của sức sống và sự dồi dào. Bản thân những cái cây đã có sự hợp tác đáng chú ý. Cây cọ dầu phát triển mạnh ở những khu vực bị đốt phá và phát quang, điều đó có nghĩa là [âm nhạc] ở bất cứ nơi đâu có con người được trồng trọt và di chuyển, những lùm cọ sẽ mọc lên trên vùng đất bị bỏ hoang. Các ngôi làng cũ [âm nhạc] và các trang trại cũ đã trở thành những cụm cây cọ dày đặc qua nhiều năm. Nhiều đến mức cho đến tận ngày nay, sự phân bố của cây cọ dầu hoang dã trên khắp miền Tây Châu Phi [âm nhạc] lập bản đồ gần như hoàn hảo về vị trí của các khu định cư cổ xưa. Bạn có thể đi bộ xuyên qua một khu rừng ở khu vực ngày nay là miền nam Nigeria hoặc [âm nhạc] Cameroon và đọc lịch sử cư trú của con người chỉ bằng cách nhìn vào nơi lòng bàn tay mọc lên.
